items.q: According to the Canadian C-spine rule, which of the following is considered a high-risk factor that mandates cervical spine imaging without assessing active range of motion?
o: Ability to rotate the neck 45 degrees bilaterally
items.e: Under the Canadian C-spine rule, high-risk criteria requiring imaging include age 65 years or older, a dangerous mechanism of injury, and paresthesias in the extremities. Patients without high-risk factors can proceed to low-risk assessment and range-of-motion testing.
items.note: Accurate, well-constructed question testing standard Canadian C-spine rule criteria.

items.q: On an open-mouth odontoid radiograph of a patient with a suspected C1 burst (Jefferson) fracture, a combined lateral mass overhang exceeding which threshold suggests disruption of the transverse atlantal ligament (Rule of Spence)?
items.e: According to the Rule of Spence, a combined overhang of the lateral masses of C1 on C2 greater than 6.9 mm (approximately 7 mm, or 8.1 mm with radiographic magnification) indicates rupture of the transverse atlantal ligament, signifying an unstable atlas injury.
items.note: Classic exam concept and exact numerical threshold from standard spine literature.

items.q: In the Grauer modification of Anderson-D'Alonzo type II odontoid fractures, which fracture pattern represents a contraindication to an anterior odontoid screw because the screw trajectory would shear the fracture line, making posterior C1-C2 fusion preferable?
o: Oblique fracture from anterosuperior to posteroinferior (Type IIB)
Oblique fracture from anteroinferior to posterosuperior (Type IIC)
Fracture extending into the cancellous body of C2 (Type III)
items.e: Grauer type IIC fractures slope from anteroinferior to posterosuperior (or are comminuted), which predisposes to shear displacement during anterior screw insertion; thus, posterior C1-C2 fusion is indicated. In contrast, type IIB fractures (anterosuperior to posteroinferior) are perpendicular to the screw trajectory.
items.note: Factually precise modification of Anderson-D'Alonzo classification frequently tested in SS exams.

items.q: A 30-year-old unrestrained driver sustains a traumatic spondylolisthesis of the axis (Hangman's fracture) featuring severe C2-C3 angulation with minimal translation caused by a flexion-distraction mechanism (Levine-Edwards type IIA). Which intervention is strictly contraindicated in this patient?
o: Closed reduction in extension and gentle compression
items.e: In Levine-Edwards type IIA fractures, the C2-C3 disc and posterior ligamentous complex are disrupted by flexion-distraction. Applying traction will worsen disc distraction and neurological risk; reduction is achieved with gentle compression and extension, followed by halo immobilisation.
items.note: High-yield emergency management concept with absolute contraindication clearly supported by text.

items.q: A 26-year-old male presents following a motor vehicle collision with an acute bilateral C5-C6 facet dislocation and an incomplete spinal cord injury. He is awake, alert, and fully cooperative. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
o: Closed traction reduction without obtaining a pre-reduction MRI
Urgent pre-reduction MRI to rule out disc herniation
Emergent posterior open reduction without attempting closed traction
Rigid cervical collar immobilisation and observation
items.e: In an awake, alert, and cooperative patient, closed traction reduction using incremental weights is safe and effective without a pre-reduction MRI. Pre-reduction MRI is indicated when the patient is obtunded, uncooperative, or when closed reduction fails.
items.note: Standard guideline-backed decision point in acute subaxial facet dislocations.

items.q: According to the Subaxial Injury Classification and Severity (SLIC) score for cervical trauma, what is the threshold total score that clearly indicates operative management?
items.e: In the SLIC system, a total score under 4 indicates non-operative management, a score of 4 is managed at the surgeon's discretion, and a score of 5 or more (over 4) indicates the need for surgical stabilisation.
items.note: Standard classification question with clear numerical cutoff.

items.q: In a complete cervical spinal cord injury, which key neurological level must be preserved to provide active elbow extension (triceps function), representing the critical milestone for independent wheelchair transfers?
items.e: C7 innervates the triceps (elbow extension), making it the critical functional level that allows patients with complete tetraplegia to achieve independent transfers and manual wheelchair propulsion without adaptations. C6 preserves wrist extension (tenodesis), while C5 provides elbow flexion.
items.note: High-yield rehabilitation and functional spinal cord injury milestone question.

items.q: A 22-year-old unrestrained driver sustains a flexion-compression cervical injury. Imaging shows an anteroinferior triangular vertebral body fragment of C5, posterior displacement of the vertebral body into the canal, and disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex. Neurological examination reveals complete loss of motor function and pain/temperature sensation below C5, with intact dorsal column proprioception and vibration. What is the injury pattern?
o: Extension teardrop fracture with posterior cord syndrome
Flexion teardrop fracture with anterior cord syndrome
Jefferson burst fracture with central cord syndrome
items.e: Flexion teardrop fractures result from flexion-compression, producing a characteristic anteroinferior fragment, retropulsion of the body into the canal, and posterior ligament rupture; they are highly unstable and commonly cause anterior cord syndrome with motor and spinothalamic loss but preserved dorsal columns.
items.note: Classic clinicoradiological vignette matching teardrop fracture and incomplete cord syndrome.

items.q: According to Denis's three-column concept of thoracolumbar spinal stability, which of the following structures is included in the middle column?
o: Posterior third of the vertebral body and posterior longitudinal ligament
Anterior two-thirds of the vertebral body and anterior longitudinal ligament
Pedicles, neural arch, and facet joint capsules
items.e: In Denis's three-column concept, the middle column comprises the posterior third of the vertebral body, posterior third of the intervertebral disc, and the posterior longitudinal ligament (PLL). Disruption of the middle column is the key determinant of mechanical instability in Denis's model.
items.note: Accurate, clear single-best-answer question directly testing Denis's three-column breakdown.

items.q: In the AO Spine thoracolumbar classification system, an injury showing posterior ligamentous tension band disruption combined with a vertebral body fracture (Type A injury pattern) is classified as:
items.e: In the AO Spine classification, Type B2 represents disruption of the posterior ligamentous tension band combined with any Type A vertebral body fracture. Type B1 is a transosseous tension band failure (bony Chance), while Type B3 is a hyperextension injury.
items.note: Direct, standard question on the 2013 AO Spine classification scheme.

items.q: A 25-year-old man falls from a height and sustains an L1 burst fracture (AO Type A3). Neurological examination is completely intact (ASIA E). MRI demonstrates an intact posterior ligamentous complex (PLC), 35% retropulsion into the spinal canal, and 15 degrees of local kyphosis. Based on evidence from prospective trials (such as Wood et al.), what is the most appropriate management?
items.e: Randomized evidence (Wood et al.) demonstrates that neurologically intact patients with burst fractures and an intact PLC have similar long-term outcomes with non-operative management (early mobilization with or without a brace) compared to surgery. Canal retropulsion and kyphosis alone do not force surgical intervention as retropulsed bone fragments resorb over time.
items.note: Evidence-based question directly backed by randomized trial data referenced in standard orthopaedic texts.

items.q: A 20-year-old rear-seat passenger wearing only a lap belt sustains an L2 flexion-distraction (Chance) fracture. Which associated non-spinal injury occurs in approximately 40% to 50% of patients presenting with this fracture pattern?
items.e: Flexion-distraction (Chance) injuries caused by lap-belt restraint are associated with intra-abdominal visceral injuries (such as bowel perforations and mesenteric tears) in 40-50% of cases, often signaled clinically by a abdominal 'seat-belt sign'.
items.note: High-yield classic association question testing standard trauma knowledge.

items.q: A 74-year-old osteoporotic female presents with worsening low back pain six weeks after a fall from standing height. Radiographs and MRI demonstrate delayed post-traumatic collapse of the L1 vertebral body containing an intravertebral vacuum cleft due to avascular necrosis. What is the eponym for this condition?
items.e: Kümmell disease is defined as delayed post-traumatic vertebral osteonecrosis and collapse, classically characterized by an intravertebral vacuum cleft on imaging. Scheuermann disease involves juvenile kyphosis, while Pott disease is tuberculous spondylodiscitis.
items.note: Fixed a minor grammatical typo in the stem ('An 74-year-old' to 'A 74-year-old'). The question tests a landmark eponym.

items.q: In thoracolumbar spinal trauma, the thoracic spinal cord is especially susceptible to vascular compromise and complete neurological injury because of its narrow canal and tenuous blood supply. Which segmental region represents the vascular watershed zone of the thoracic spinal cord?
items.e: The thoracic cord blood supply is most vulnerable at the T4–T9 watershed region. Because of this tenuous vascularity and the narrow thoracic canal, trauma in this region results in a higher proportion of complete spinal cord injuries.
items.note: Standard anatomical/biomechanical question.

items.q: When assessing a thoracolumbar burst fracture for posterior short-segment pedicle screw fixation, an anterior corpectomy and reconstruction is indicated if the McCormack Load-Sharing Classification score reaches or exceeds:
items.e: A McCormack Load-Sharing Classification score of 7 or more indicates severe vertebral body comminution, fragment displacement, and kyphosis correction requirements, signifying that posterior short-segment fixation alone is prone to failure and anterior column reconstruction is required.
items.note: Standard scoring system question with clear numerical cutoff.

items.q: A 56-year-old male presents with difficulty buttoning his shirt and hand numbness. Examination reveals hyperreflexia and finger flexion with diminished brachioradialis contraction when tapping the brachioradialis tendon (inverted brachioradialis reflex). At which spinal level is the primary compressive lesion located?
items.e: The inverted brachioradialis (radial) reflex is characterized by finger flexion and reduced brachioradialis contraction upon tapping the brachioradialis tendon, which localizes the pathology to the C5-C6 spinal level.
items.note: Accurate localization classic for Indian orthopaedic entrance exams; supported by standard reference text.

items.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of clumsy hands and gait imbalance. Clinical examination demonstrates a positive Hoffmann sign, broad-based spastic gait, and hyperreflexia. His modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score is calculated to be 13. According to the AO Spine / WFNS guidelines, what is the recommended management?
o: Supervised trial of structured rehabilitation for 6 months
Strict immobilisation in a rigid cervical collar for 12 weeks
Observation with repeat clinical evaluation in 1 year
items.e: According to the AO Spine / WFNS guidelines (Fehlings 2017), surgical decompression is recommended for patients with moderate (mJOA score 12-14) and severe (mJOA score under 12) degenerative cervical myelopathy.
items.note: Direct clinical application of AO Spine / WFNS guidelines for DCM management.

items.q: On a lateral cervical spine radiograph, sagittal canal stenosis is evaluated using the Torg-Pavlov ratio and absolute anteroposterior (AP) canal diameter. Which of the following values represents absolute cervical spinal canal stenosis?
o: Torg-Pavlov ratio under 0.8 and absolute AP canal diameter under 10 mm
Torg-Pavlov ratio over 1.0 and absolute AP canal diameter under 13 mm
Torg-Pavlov ratio under 0.8 and absolute AP canal diameter between 13 and 15 mm
Torg-Pavlov ratio over 0.8 and absolute AP canal diameter over 15 mm
items.e: A Torg-Pavlov ratio under 0.8 indicates canal stenosis. An absolute AP canal diameter under 13 mm represents relative stenosis, whereas an AP diameter under 10 mm defines absolute canal stenosis.
items.note: Standard radiological threshold question with single unequivocal correct answer.

items.q: A patient with degenerative cervical myelopathy undergoes MRI evaluation of the spinal cord. Which intramedullary signal pattern indicates irreversible cord myelomalacia and carries the worst functional prognosis post-operatively?
o: Combined T1-weighted hypointensity and T2-weighted hyperintensity
Isointense T1 and T2 signal with peripheral rim enhancement
items.e: T2-weighted hyperintensity alone may reflect reversible cord oedema. However, combined T1-weighted hypointensity and T2-weighted hyperintensity indicates cord myelomalacia or cavitation, which is irreversible and predicts a worse prognosis.
items.note: Classic neuroimaging prognostic factor question in spinal surgery.

items.q: A CT scan in a patient with ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) reveals a 'double-layer sign' behind the C5 vertebral body. What is the primary surgical risk associated with this radiological finding during anterior decompression?
o: High probability of vertebral artery injury
Increased risk of dural tear and CSF leakage
Complete immunity from post-operative C5 nerve root palsy
Inability to achieve solid interbody fusion
items.e: The 'double-layer sign' on CT suggests dural ossification, which significantly increases the risk of a dural tear and CSF leak during anterior resection of the OPLL.
items.note: High-yield surgical anatomy and complication question specific to OPLL management.

items.q: Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) is classified into four anatomical patterns based on CT and radiographic appearance. Which of the following is the most common pattern of OPLL?
items.e: The segmental pattern is the commonest subtype of OPLL, characterized by ossification behind the vertebral bodies at disc spaces without continuity.
items.note: Standard classification question regarding OPLL epidemiology and imaging.

items.q: Open-door laminoplasty (Hirabayashi technique) relies on the posterior drift of the spinal cord for indirect decompression. Which of the following anatomical findings is an absolute contraindication to performing laminoplasty alone?
items.e: Laminoplasty relies on dorsal drift of the spinal cord away from anterior compression, which requires preserved cervical lordosis (or K-line positive status). Fixed cervical kyphosis is a contraindication because the cord cannot drift posteriorly.
items.note: Crucial surgical indication/contraindication question frequently tested in SS exams.

items.q: Two days following posterior cervical laminectomy and fusion, a patient develops new-onset deltoid weakness without any sensory loss or lower limb deterioration. What is the expected clinical course and primary mechanism of this complication?
o: Direct intra-operative root transection; permanent motor deficit expected
Tethering of the C5 nerve root due to dorsal cord drift; most patients recover spontaneously within 6 to 12 months
Progressive intramedullary cord ischemia; requires emergency anterior revision surgery
Brachial plexus traction from positioning; complete resolution expected within 48 hours
items.e: Post-operative C5 palsy presents as deltoid ± biceps weakness appearing hours to days after surgery, primarily caused by tethering of the C5 root as the spinal cord drifts dorsally. Most patients recover spontaneously within 6 to 12 months.
items.note: Classic post-decompression complication question testing mechanism and prognosis.

items.q: A 42-year-old male with persistent low back pain undergoes an MRI of the lumbar spine, which demonstrates T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense signal changes in the endplate bone marrow at L4-L5. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathology of these Modic Type I changes?
o: Bone marrow oedema and active inflammation
items.e: Modic Type I endplate changes show low T1 and high T2 signal on MRI, representing bone marrow oedema and active inflammation. These changes are most strongly associated with active low back pain.
items.note: Accurate, well-constructed question testing standard Modic classification definitions directly backed by reference notes.

items.q: A 45-year-old female presents with severe right leg radiculopathy. An MRI reveals a far lateral (foraminal) disc herniation at the L4-L5 level. Which nerve root is directly compressed by this herniation?
items.e: A far lateral (foraminal) disc herniation at L4-L5 compresses the exiting L4 nerve root. In contrast, a typical paracentral herniation at L4-L5 compresses the traversing L5 nerve root.
items.note: High-yield standard spinal neurology distinction (exiting vs traversing nerve roots) fully supported by notes.

items.q: To avoid an extensive facetectomy during surgery for a far lateral lumbar disc herniation, which surgical approach utilizes a muscle-splitting plane between the multifidus and longissimus muscles?
items.e: The Wiltse paraspinal muscle-splitting approach operates between the multifidus and longissimus muscles. It allows direct access to far lateral (extraforaminal) herniations without requiring facetectomy.
items.note: Classic subspecialty surgical approach question, factually accurate and well-phrased.

items.q: A patient undergoing spinal surgery for lumbar central stenosis is being evaluated for whether decompression alone or decompression with fusion is indicated. Which feature on dynamic flexion-extension radiographs favors adding fusion to decompression?
o: Dynamic sagittal translation greater than 3 to 4 mm
Complete collapse of intervertebral disc height
Sclerotic Modic Type III endplate changes
items.e: Adding fusion to decompression is indicated when dynamic instability is demonstrated on flexion-extension radiographs, defined as dynamic translation greater than 3 to 4 mm or angulation greater than 10 to 15 degrees.
items.note: Standard surgical indication question based on established radiographic parameters of segmental instability.

items.q: A 38-year-old male presents with acute bilateral leg pain, saddle altered sensation, and difficulty initiating urination with a weak stream. Post-void bladder scanning reveals a residual volume of 80 mL (no urinary retention). How is this condition classified?
items.e: Incomplete cauda equina syndrome (CES-I) is characterized by altered urinary sensation, reduced desire to void, or poor stream, but without frank painless urinary retention with overflow (which defines CES-R). Decompression before retention yields superior clinical outcomes.
items.note: Clinically relevant classification question on cauda equina syndrome, matching current guideline definitions.

items.q: Which anatomical feature distinguishes Type III (degenerative) spondylolisthesis from Type II (isthmic) spondylolisthesis?
o: Lytic defect in the pars interarticularis
Intact pars interarticularis with sagittal facet orientation
Most commonly affects the L5-S1 vertebral level
Presence of dysplastic facets and elongated pars
items.e: Type III (degenerative) spondylolisthesis occurs with an intact pars interarticularis and is characteristically associated with sagittal orientation of the facet joints at L4-L5 in women over 50. Type II (isthmic) involves a pars defect and most commonly affects L5-S1.
items.note: Clear diagnostic distinction based on Wiltse-Newman classification of spondylolisthesis.

items.q: Which clinical manifestation is most characteristic of vascular claudication rather than neurogenic claudication?
o: Relief of symptoms upon sitting or bending forward
Ability to cycle comfortably while walking causes leg pain
Relief of leg pain simply by standing still in an upright position
Progression of symptoms in a proximal-to-distal direction
items.e: Vascular claudication is relieved by standing still without needing to alter posture or sit down. In contrast, neurogenic claudication is exacerbated by standing upright (extension) and requires sitting or bending forward (flexion) for symptom relief.
items.note: Classic clinical differentiator between neurogenic and vascular claudication.

items.q: During a lumbar microdiscectomy, deep anterior perforation of the annulus fibrosus occurs, causing sudden heavy retroperitoneal hemorrhage and severe intraoperative hypotension. What is the immediate definitive management required?
o: Packing the disc space posteriorly with microfibrillar collagen
Immediate hyperflexion of the patient's hips and spine
items.e: Deep anterior perforation of the annulus fibrosus risks catastrophic injury to major anterior abdominal vessels (aorta, vena cava, or iliac vessels). Sudden hypotension requires immediate emergency abdominal laparotomy to achieve vascular control and repair.
items.note: Crucial surgical complication question directly verified by Campbell's Operative Orthopaedics and notes.

items.q: A 13-year-old boy presents with a progressive left thoracic scoliotic curve measuring 32 degrees Cobb angle. On clinical examination, abnormal abdominal reflexes are elicited. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Serial standing PA radiographs every 6 months to assess curve progression
Immediate prescription of a full-time Boston thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO)
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the whole neural axis
Computed tomography (CT) scan of the thoracic spine for pedicle morphometry
items.e: A left thoracic curve, abnormal abdominal reflexes, male sex with severe curve, or presence of neurological signs in scoliosis are red flags that mandate an MRI of the entire neural axis to rule out underlying neural pathologies such as a syrinx, Chiari malformation, or tethered cord.
items.note: Accurate, standard SS exam question covering red flag indications for neural axis MRI in scoliosis.

items.q: A 16-year-old male presents with rigid thoracic hyperkyphosis measuring 78 degrees that fails to correct on extension radiographs. Lateral radiographs demonstrate endplate irregularity, narrow disc spaces, and anterior wedging of 6 degrees in three adjacent thoracic vertebrae. If posterior fusion with posterior column osteotomies is performed, what is the recommended distal fusion limit to avoid distal junctional kyphosis?
items.e: In Scheuermann kyphosis requiring posterior fusion for deformity over 75 degrees, fusion should extend proximally from the upper end vertebra down to the sagittal stable vertebra to minimize the risk of developing postoperative distal junctional kyphosis.
items.note: High-yield, standard concept in Scheuermann kyphosis surgical planning.

items.q: Which of the following congenital spinal anomalies carries the worst prognosis for rapid curve progression, typically progressing at a rate of 5 to 10 degrees per year?
o: Unilateral unsegmented bar with a contralateral fully segmented hemivertebra
items.e: A unilateral unsegmented bar combined with a contralateral fully segmented hemivertebra represents the worst malignant congenital scoliosis pattern, causing rapid progression of 5 to 10 degrees per year and requiring early surgical intervention.
items.note: Classic high-yield factoid regarding congenital scoliosis prognosis.

items.q: A 14-year-old girl undergoes posterior spinal instrumentation and fusion with pedicle screws for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. On postoperative day 3, following diet advancement, she develops intractable bilious vomiting, postprandial epigastric abdominal pain, and abdominal distension. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cutibacterium acnes deep surgical site infection
items.e: Superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome occurs postoperatively after scoliosis correction due to elongation of the spine, which compresses the third part of the duodenum between the SMA and the aorta/spine, leading to bilious vomiting and bowel obstruction symptoms.
items.note: Standard postoperative complication question for scoliosis surgery.

items.q: According to the landmark BrAIST (Bracing in Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis Trial) trial by Weinstein et al. (2013), what daily brace-wear duration threshold was associated with an approximate 90% success rate in preventing curve progression to the 50-degree surgical threshold?
items.e: The BrAIST trial demonstrated a clear dose-response relationship for TLSO bracing in skeletally immature patients, showing that wearing the brace for more than 13 hours per day achieved approximately 90% success in halting curve progression to the surgical threshold of 50 degrees.
items.note: Landmark trial testing key evidence-based management threshold in AIS.

items.q: Regarding spinal osteotomies used in spinal deformity correction, which of the following statements is correct?
o: A Smith-Petersen / Ponte osteotomy provides approximately 30 to 35 degrees of correction per level.
A pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO) is a three-column closing-wedge osteotomy through the vertebra that yields approximately 30 to 35 degrees of sagittal correction.
A Vertebral Column Resection (VCR) provides 10 degrees of correction and requires a mobile anterior disc space.
A Ponte osteotomy carries the highest risk of neurological deficit among all spinal osteotomies.
items.e: A pedicle subtraction osteotomy (PSO) is a three-column closing wedge procedure performed through the vertebra (commonly L3) yielding about 30 to 35 degrees of lordotic correction. Ponte osteotomies provide ~10 degrees per level (requiring a mobile anterior disc), whereas VCR gives >40 degrees for rigid deformities and carries the highest neurological risk.
items.note: Factually precise question testing spinal osteotomy indications and degree of correction.

items.q: A 2-year-old child is diagnosed with congenital scoliosis. As part of the mandatory screening protocol for associated congenital anomalies, which of the following findings is correct regarding associated organ system involvement?
o: Genitourinary anomalies occur in about 5% of cases and never cause obstructive uropathy.
Genitourinary anomalies occur in approximately 20% of patients, and 2-3% may have life-threatening obstructive anomalies requiring screening renal ultrasound.
Intraspinal anomalies occur in less than 2% of patients, making routine spinal cord MRI unnecessary.
Echocardiography is not indicated because congenital heart defects are not associated with congenital scoliosis.
items.e: Patients with congenital scoliosis must be screened for associated organ anomalies: genitourinary anomalies occur in ~20% (with 2-3% being obstructive and life-threatening, warranting a renal ultrasound), cardiac anomalies in 10-25% (warranting echocardiography), and intraspinal anomalies in 20-40% (warranting MRI).
items.note: Accurate, practical clinical management standard for screening congenital scoliosis.

items.q: A 9-year-old skeletally immature girl with Risser stage 0 and open triradiate cartilage undergoes posterior spinal fusion alone without anterior procedures for a progressive thoracic scoliotic curve. Which complication is she at high risk of developing secondary to persistent anterior vertebral body growth?
items.e: The crankshaft phenomenon occurs when posterior fusion alone is performed in a skeletally very immature spine (Risser 0, open triradiate cartilage); ongoing anterior spinal growth around the tethered posterior elements leads to progressive rotational and coronal deformity.
items.note: Classic paediatric spine concept tested frequently in subspecialty exams.

items.q: A 34-year-old male presents with chronic back pain, weight loss, and an evening rise in temperature. Radiographs show a 'bird nest' appearance of a paravertebral shadow in the thoracic spine. What is the most likely mechanism of spread of the causative organism to this site?
o: Lymphatic spread from the thoracic duct
Haematogenous spread via Batson's venous plexus
Contiguous spread from a psoas abscess
items.e: Spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease) most commonly spreads haematogenously via the valveless vertebral venous plexus of Batson or through the arterial supply, often involving the thoracolumbar junction.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the most common route of spread and a classic radiographic sign of spinal TB as per the reference notes.

items.q: In a child with spinal tuberculosis, which of the following is one of the four 'spine-at-risk' signs described by Rajasekaran that predict severe kyphotic progression?
o: Concertina collapse of a single vertebra
Preservation of the intervertebral disc space
items.e: Rajasekaran's 'spine-at-risk' signs include separation of facets, posterior retropulsion, lateral translation, and toppling (tilt of the upper vertebra). The presence of two or more of these signs predicts severe progression of kyphosis in children.
items.note: The original question asked which sign was 'most strongly associated' when two or more are present, which is illogical as the risk is cumulative based on the number of signs. I fixed it to a direct id

items.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with lower limb weakness and sensory loss ten years after being treated for spinal tuberculosis. MRI shows a prominent internal bony ridge (internal gibbus) and cord atrophy, but no evidence of active infection. What is the most likely prognosis for neurological recovery in this patient?
o: Good prognosis with a second course of antitubercular therapy
Poor prognosis as this represents late-onset paraplegia
Excellent prognosis with bracing and rest
items.e: Late-onset Pott's paraplegia occurs years after the disease has healed, typically due to an internal gibbus or meningeal scarring. It has a poor prognosis compared to early-onset paraplegia, which is caused by active disease factors like abscess or granulation tissue.
items.note: The question accurately distinguishes between early and late-onset Pott's paraplegia and their respective prognoses as per the reference notes.

items.q: Which MRI feature is most characteristic of pyogenic spondylodiscitis rather than tuberculous spondylitis?
o: Relative preservation of the intervertebral disc early in the disease
Large paraspinal abscess with a thin, smooth enhancing wall
Early destruction of the intervertebral disc and T2 hyperintensity
Presence of skip lesions across multiple non-contiguous levels
items.e: In pyogenic infections, the disc is destroyed early because the infection often starts in the subchondral endplate and spreads quickly into the disc. In TB, the disc is relatively preserved early in the disease course.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the key MRI differentiator between pyogenic and tuberculous spinal infections.

items.q: A patient being treated for spinal tuberculosis with the standard WHO/NTEP regimen (HRZE) complains of new-onset blurring of vision and inability to distinguish red from green. Which drug should be immediately evaluated for toxicity?
items.e: Ethambutol is known to cause optic neuritis, which manifests as decreased visual acuity and red-green color blindness. Isoniazid is more commonly associated with peripheral neuropathy.
items.note: The question tests a classic and high-yield drug side effect mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: A 58-year-old diabetic male presents with severe back pain, high-grade fever, and acute onset of complete paraplegia over the last 12 hours. MRI shows a posterior spinal epidural abscess from T10 to L2. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Immediate CT-guided needle aspiration and IV antibiotics
Complete bed rest and 6 weeks of targeted IV antibiotics
Observation for 48 hours to assess for spontaneous recovery
items.e: Urgent surgical decompression and drainage is the treatment of choice for spinal epidural abscess with a neurological deficit. Prognosis is poor if paralysis lasts longer than 24-36 hours.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the surgical emergency and management protocol for spinal epidural abscess with neurological deficit.

items.q: A 40-year-old farmer presents with chronic back pain and radiographs showing erosion of the anterosuperior endplate of the L3 vertebra (Pedro Pons sign). He mentions consuming raw camel milk. What is the most likely causative organism?
items.e: Brucellosis is an endemic infection (often from farm animals or raw milk) that causes spondylodiscitis. The Pedro Pons sign (anterosuperior endplate erosion) is a classic radiographic feature.
items.note: The question uses a specific eponym and clinical history that points directly to Brucella as per the reference notes.

items.q: According to the study by Bernard et al. (Lancet 2015), what is the recommended duration of antibiotic therapy for pyogenic spondylodiscitis that is as effective as a 12-week course?
items.e: Bernard et al. (2015) demonstrated that 6 weeks of antibiotic treatment is as effective as 12 weeks for pyogenic spondylodiscitis, reducing the duration of treatment for most patients.
items.note: The question tests a specific, evidence-based guideline mentioned in the reference notes regarding the duration of treatment for pyogenic infection.

items.q: A 62-year-old male with a history of weight loss and back pain is diagnosed with metastatic spine disease. Statistically, which region of the spine is the most likely site for these metastases?
items.e: The spine is the most common site of skeletal metastasis, with the thoracic spine being the most common region involved (approximately 70%), followed by the lumbar and cervical regions.

items.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with painful scoliosis. Imaging reveals a small nidus in the posterior elements of the L3 vertebra on the concave side of the curve. The pain is significantly relieved by aspirin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
items.e: Osteoid osteoma typically occurs in young males, involves the posterior elements, and causes painful scoliosis where the lesion is located on the concave side of the apex. The pain is characteristically relieved by NSAIDs.

items.q: According to the Bilsky scale for Epidural Spinal Cord Compression (ESCC) used in the NOMS framework, how is a lesion classified when there is cord compression but cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) remains visible?
items.e: Bilsky Grade 2 represents spinal cord compression where CSF is still visible. Grade 3 is cord compression with no CSF visible (total obliteration), while Grade 1c is cord abutment without compression.

items.q: In the Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS), which of the following vertebral levels would be assigned the highest score (3 points) for 'Location'?
items.e: Junctional locations (C0-C2, C7-T2, T11-L1, L5-S1) score 3 points in the SINS. T12 falls in the T11-L1 junctional zone. Mobile spine (C3-C6, L2-L4) scores 2, and semi-rigid (T3-T10) scores 1.

items.q: A 55-year-old patient is scheduled for surgical stabilization of a solitary, hypervascular metastatic lesion at T10. Which primary tumor source would most likely necessitate pre-operative embolization to reduce intraoperative blood loss?
items.e: Metastases from renal cell carcinoma and thyroid carcinoma are highly vascular and typically require pre-operative embolization (usually within 48 hours of surgery) to manage bleeding risk.

items.q: Which of the following tumors is classified as 'radioresistant' to conventional external beam radiotherapy in the NOMS framework?
items.e: Radioresistant tumors include renal cell carcinoma, melanoma, thyroid carcinoma, sarcoma, GI (colon), and NSCLC. Myeloma, lymphoma, breast, and prostate are considered radiosensitive.

items.q: The landmark randomized trial by Patchell et al. (2005) demonstrated that for patients with metastatic spinal cord compression from solid tumors:
o: Radiotherapy alone is superior to surgery in preserving ambulation.
Direct decompressive surgery followed by radiotherapy is superior to radiotherapy alone.
Surgery is only indicated if the patient has been paraplegic for over 48 hours.
Steroids alone are as effective as surgery for radioresistant tumors.
items.e: The Patchell trial showed that surgery plus radiotherapy was superior to radiotherapy alone for MSCC from solid tumors; 84% of the surgery group could walk post-treatment compared to 57% in the radiotherapy-only group.

items.q: A 60-year-old male presents with a large, lytic, midline destructive lesion of the sacrum. Biopsy reveals physaliferous cells and brachyury positivity. What is the management of choice for this primary malignant tumor?
o: Radiotherapy alone as it is highly radiosensitive
En bloc resection with wide margins
items.e: Chordomas are midline tumors (most common in sacrum and clivus) characterized by physaliferous cells and brachyury expression. They are radioresistant to conventional RT and require en bloc resection with wide margins to prevent high rates of local recurrence.

items.q: Which of the following statements regarding pelvic incidence (PI) is correct according to the geometric relationships of spinopelvic alignment?
o: PI is a positional parameter that increases when a patient sits down
PI is calculated as the sum of pelvic tilt (PT) and sacral slope (SS)
PI decreases significantly during the compensatory phase of sagittal malalignment
PI is the angle between the S1 endplate and the horizontal line
items.e: Pelvic incidence (PI) is a fixed morphological parameter after skeletal maturity and does not change with position. Geometrically, PI is the sum of pelvic tilt (PT) and sacral slope (SS).
items.note: The question accurately tests the fundamental geometric relationship of pelvic parameters as defined in the reference notes.

items.q: A 65-year-old male presents with severe sagittal malalignment. He is noted to be standing with his knees flexed and ankles dorsiflexed to maintain an upright posture. According to the stages of compensation, which mechanism occurs immediately before the recruitment of knee flexion?
items.e: The body compensates for sagittal malalignment in a specific sequence: thoracic hypokyphosis, lumbar hyperextension, and then pelvic retroversion (increased PT). Knee flexion and ankle dorsiflexion are recruited once pelvic retroversion reaches its limit (hip extension reserve).
items.note: The question correctly identifies the sequence of compensatory mechanisms in sagittal malalignment as described in the reference notes.

items.q: According to the SRS-Schwab sagittal modifiers, which of the following measurements would be classified as a '++' (marked) deformity?
items.e: In the SRS-Schwab classification, a '++' modifier is assigned for PI-LL > 20°, PT > 30°, or SVA > 9.5 cm. A PT of 35 degrees meets this criteria.
items.note: The question correctly applies the SRS-Schwab classification thresholds for sagittal modifiers.

items.q: A 35-year-old patient with chronic low back pain is evaluated using the Roussouly classification. Radiographs reveal a sacral slope of 28 degrees and a flat, long hypolordotic lumbar spine. This sagittal profile is most strongly associated with which pathology?
items.e: Roussouly Type 2 is characterized by a sacral slope < 35 degrees and a flat, hypolordotic lumbar spine. This 'flat back' profile is associated with increased risks of disc herniation and early disc degeneration.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the Roussouly Type 2 profile and its associated clinical pathology.

items.q: Which of the following is considered a risk factor for the development of proximal junctional kyphosis (PJK) following long-segment spinal fusion?
o: Upper Instrumented Vertebra (UIV) at the thoracolumbar junction
Under-correction of sagittal alignment in elderly patients
items.e: Risk factors for PJK include older age, osteoporosis, large corrections, high BMI, fusion to the sacrum, and having the Upper Instrumented Vertebra (UIV) located at the thoracolumbar junction.
items.note: The question correctly identifies a well-established risk factor for PJK as listed in the reference notes.

items.q: A patient with a history of lumbar spine fusion presents for a total hip arthroplasty (THA). How does a stiff or fused spine affect the mechanics of the hip when the patient moves from a standing to a sitting position?
o: The pelvis fails to retrovert, increasing the risk of THA dislocation
The pelvis retroverts excessively, leading to anterior impingement
Sacral slope increases during sitting, improving cup cover
The spine-hip relationship is only relevant in the coronal plane
items.e: Normally, sitting causes the pelvis to retrovert (tilt posteriorly) by about 20 degrees, which increases functional cup anteversion. A stiff spine prevents this retroversion, increasing the risk of THA dislocation and impingement.
items.note: The question correctly addresses the hip-spine syndrome and its implications for THA stability.

items.q: When planning a corrective osteotomy for a patient with ankylosing spondylitis and a severe 'chin-on-chest' deformity, which parameter is most important for restoring horizontal gaze?
items.e: The chin-brow vertical angle (CBVA) is the most important parameter for planning horizontal gaze restoration in ankylosing spondylitis; the target is typically 0-10 degrees.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the clinical parameter used for horizontal gaze assessment in spinal deformity surgery.

items.q: During a direct lateral (Hardinge) approach for total hip arthroplasty, a surgeon splits the gluteus medius. To avoid injury to the superior gluteal nerve, the split should not extend more than how many centimeters proximal to the tip of the greater trochanter?
items.e: In the direct lateral (Hardinge) approach, the superior gluteal nerve is at risk if the gluteus medius split extends more than 5 cm proximal to the tip of the greater trochanter; injury results in abductor weakness and a Trendelenburg gait.
items.note: The 5 cm threshold is a standard anatomical landmark cited in Campbell's to protect the superior gluteal nerve during this approach.

items.q: A 74-year-old male presents with a periprosthetic femoral fracture one year after a THA. Radiographs show the fracture is around the stem, and the stem appears loose with subsidence and radiolucent lines, but the bone stock is relatively preserved. According to the Vancouver classification, what is the treatment of choice?
o: ORIF with a locking plate and cables
Revision with a long stem bypassing the fracture
Non-operative management with a hip spica
items.e: This is a Vancouver B2 fracture (loose stem, good bone stock), which requires revision with a long stem to achieve distal fixation, bypassing the fracture by at least two cortical diameters.
items.note: The clinical description matches a Vancouver B2 fracture exactly, for which long-stem revision is the gold standard.

items.q: In the Wasielewski quadrant system for acetabular screw placement, which quadrant is referred to as the 'death zone' due to the proximity of the external iliac artery and vein?
items.e: The anterosuperior quadrant is the 'death zone' because the external iliac artery and vein lie directly adjacent to the bone in this area. The posterosuperior quadrant is considered the safest for screw placement.
items.note: The Wasielewski quadrant system is the standard for identifying safe zones for acetabular screws; the anterosuperior quadrant contains the external iliac vessels.

items.q: A patient experiences persistent numbness and tingling over the anterolateral aspect of the thigh following a total hip arthroplasty. This complication is most frequently associated with which surgical approach?
items.e: The direct anterior approach (DAA) carries a high risk (up to 15-80%) of transient numbness due to injury or traction of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (meralgia paraesthetica).
items.note: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury is a classic and common complication specifically associated with the direct anterior approach.

items.q: During preoperative templating for a patient with significant limb shortening due to hip arthritis, the surgeon aims to restore leg length. According to the provided notes, lengthening the limb beyond what threshold significantly increases the risk of sciatic nerve palsy?
items.e: Restoring leg length is critical, but lengthening over approximately 2-4 cm risks sciatic nerve palsy, particularly affecting the peroneal division.
items.note: The 4 cm threshold is the widely accepted upper limit in orthopaedic literature beyond which the risk of sciatic nerve palsy becomes significantly elevated.

items.q: A 68-year-old female with a Ranawat Type II valgus deformity is undergoing TKA. During femoral preparation, the surgeon identifies significant hypoplasia of the lateral femoral condyle. Relying solely on the posterior condylar axis (PCA) for femoral component rotation in this case would most likely result in:
o: Excessive external rotation of the femoral component
Internal rotation of the femoral component and patellar maltracking
Overstuffing of the flexion gap medially
items.e: In a valgus knee with a hypoplastic lateral femoral condyle, the posterior condylar axis (PCA) is an unreliable landmark; using it typically results in internal rotation of the femoral component, leading to patellar subluxation or tilt. The transepicondylar axis (TEA) or Whiteside’s line are more reliable landmarks in this scenario.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the risk of using PCA in valgus knees as per standard arthroplasty principles and the provided notes.

items.q: During a TKA for a patient with a 15-degree fixed flexion deformity, the surgeon finds that the extension gap is tight while the flexion gap is perfectly balanced with a 10 mm trial. After removing all posterior osteophytes and performing a posterior capsular release, the extension gap remains tight. What is the next most appropriate step?
o: Downsize the femoral component and use anterior referencing
Resect an additional 2 mm of the distal femur
Release the superficial medial collateral ligament
items.e: When the knee is tight in extension but balanced in flexion, the recommended sequence is to remove posterior osteophytes and release the posterior capsule; if it remains tight, more distal femur should be resected. Resecting more tibia would affect both gaps, and downsizing the femur would only affect the flexion gap.
items.note: The management algorithm for gap balancing is a core TKA concept and matches the provided reference notes exactly.

items.q: In a TKA for a fixed varus deformity, which of the following represents the correct sequential order for medial soft-tissue release after the removal of medial osteophytes?
o: Superficial MCL, then Deep MCL, then Semimembranosus
Deep MCL, then Posteromedial capsule/Semimembranosus, then Superficial MCL
Pes anserinus, then IT band, then Deep MCL
Posteromedial capsule, then PCL, then Medial tibial reduction osteotomy
items.e: The standard release for a varus knee starts with removing medial osteophytes, followed by the deep MCL (meniscotibial), then the posteromedial capsule and semimembranosus (tight in extension), and finally the superficial MCL (anterior part for flexion, posterior part for extension).
items.note: The sequence is standard in Campbell's and correctly reflected in the options.

items.q: A surgeon is utilizing the CPAK (Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee) classification to plan a functional alignment TKA. This classification system categorizes knees into 9 phenotypes based on which two variables?
o: Mechanical HKA and Posterior Tibial Slope
Anatomical axis and Femoral neck-shaft angle
Arithmetic HKA and Joint Line Obliquity
items.e: The CPAK classification uses the arithmetic HKA (calculated from MPTA and LDFA) and the Joint Line Obliquity to describe the constitutional alignment of the knee, allowing surgeons to categorize the patient into one of nine phenotypes.
items.note: This is a modern, high-yield classification mentioned in the reference notes for functional alignment.

items.q: Following the correction of a severe valgus deformity and a significant flexion contracture during TKA, a patient is found to have a peroneal nerve palsy in the recovery room. According to recommended protocols, what is the first step in management?
o: Immediate surgical exploration of the nerve
Place the knee in extension and apply a compression bandage
Flex the knee and loosen all restrictive dressings
items.e: Peroneal nerve palsy after valgus and flexion deformity correction is often due to a stretch injury. The immediate management involves flexing the knee to reduce tension on the nerve and loosening any tight dressings; exploration is reserved for cases that do not show recovery.
items.note: This is the standard emergency management protocol for post-operative nerve palsy in TKA.

items.q: A 72-year-old patient with a history of childhood polio presents with severe tricompartmental osteoarthritis and a significant neuromuscular recurvatum (hyperextension) deformity. Which TKA design is most appropriate to provide the necessary stability?
items.e: A rotating-hinge (linked) prosthesis is indicated for global ligamentous deficiency, severe bone loss, or neuromuscular recurvatum (such as in polio) where non-linked constrained implants (CCK) may fail to prevent hyperextension.
items.note: The indication for a linked hinge in neuromuscular recurvatum is a classic exam fact.

items.q: Regarding tibial component preparation in TKA, which of the following statements is true regarding the posterior slope?
o: Cruciate-retaining (CR) knees generally require less slope than PS knees
Excessive slope in a PS knee increases the risk of cam-post impingement and instability
Increasing the slope is a recommended solution for a knee that is tight in extension
The tibial cut only affects the extension gap
items.e: In PS knees, excessive posterior slope can lead to early cam-post engagement, impingement, or flexion instability. CR knees require more slope (3-7 degrees) to maintain the flexion gap, while the tibial cut itself affects both the flexion and extension gaps.
items.note: The question tests the nuances of slope in different TKA designs, which is critical for gap balancing.

items.q: A 65-year-old male presents 2 years after a total knee arthroplasty with a draining sinus on the lateral aspect of the knee that communicates with the prosthesis. According to the 2018 ICM (International Consensus Meeting) criteria, what is the next step to confirm the diagnosis of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI)?
o: Joint aspiration for alpha-defensin and leukocyte esterase
No further tests are needed; the diagnosis is already confirmed
Frozen section histology to count neutrophils per high-power field
items.e: According to the 2018 ICM criteria, a sinus tract communicating with the joint or visualization of the prosthesis is a major criterion. The presence of even one major criterion is sufficient to diagnose PJI.
items.note: The question accurately tests the major criteria of the 2018 ICM definition as stated in the reference notes.

items.q: In the 2018 ICM definition of periprosthetic joint infection, which of the following pre-operative minor criteria is assigned the highest weight of 3 points?
items.e: Under the 2018 ICM scoring system, positive alpha-defensin and synovial WBC > 3,000 cells/µL (or leukocyte esterase ++) are each assigned 3 points. Serum CRP and synovial PMN% are worth 2 points each, while ESR and synovial CRP are worth 1 point.
items.note: The scoring weights match the 2018 ICM table provided in the reference notes.

items.q: A patient returns 2 weeks after a total hip arthroplasty with wound erythema and persistent drainage. You suspect early post-operative PJI. Which of the following synovial fluid thresholds is used to define infection in this early post-operative period (within 6 weeks) according to ICM guidelines?
items.e: Thresholds for PJI are higher in the early post-operative period (within 6 weeks) due to surgical inflammation. In this window, the thresholds are CRP > 100 mg/L, synovial WBC > 10,000 cells/µL, and PMN > 90%.
items.note: The question correctly identifies the specific thresholds for the early post-operative period as per the ICM 2018 guidelines mentioned in the notes.

items.q: What is the primary biological rationale for performing Debridement, Antibiotics, and Implant Retention (DAIR) only in patients with symptoms lasting less than 3 to 4 weeks?
o: Host cells successfully win the 'race for the surface' after 4 weeks
Bacterial biofilm matures and becomes highly resistant to antibiotics within this window
Surgical trauma prevents the safe removal of components after the first month
Synovial fluid CRP levels normalize after 4 weeks, masking the infection
items.e: Biofilm matures within about 3-4 weeks, making sessile bacteria up to 1,000 times more resistant to antibiotics. This maturation is the basis for limiting DAIR to early post-operative or acute haematogenous infections.
items.note: The question tests the fundamental concept of biofilm maturation and its impact on surgical decision-making in PJI.

items.q: A patient with poorly controlled diabetes is scheduled for total knee arthroplasty. Which of the following perioperative parameters is specifically identified in the source notes as a risk factor for PJI?
items.e: Risk factors for PJI include HbA1c over 7.5-8%, perioperative glucose over 200 mg/dL, BMI over 40 (obesity), and malnutrition markers like albumin under 3.5 g/dL.
items.note: The question tests specific risk factor thresholds defined in the provided reference material.

items.q: A 70-year-old female with a well-functioning THA performed 5 years ago presents with a 10-day history of sudden onset hip pain and fever following a urinary tract infection. Aspiration confirms S. aureus PJI. What is the most appropriate management according to management-oriented classifications?
o: DAIR with modular component exchange and rifampicin-based combination therapy
Two-stage exchange with a static spacer
items.e: This is an acute haematogenous infection (symptoms < 3 weeks) with a previously well-functioning joint. DAIR with exchange of modular parts is indicated. Rifampicin is added for staphylococcal infections with retained implants to target biofilm.
items.note: The clinical scenario matches the indications for DAIR as described in the Tsukayama classification and ICM guidelines.

items.q: Regarding antibiotic prophylaxis for primary total joint arthroplasty, which of the following practices is recommended in the source notes to minimize the risk of PJI?
o: Administer Cefazolin within 120 minutes before incision
Continue prophylactic antibiotics for 72 hours post-operatively
Redose Cefazolin if the procedure lasts longer than 4 hours
Use vancomycin as the first-line agent for all patients regardless of allergy status
items.e: Cefazolin should be given within 60 minutes of incision and redosed if the procedure exceeds 4 hours or blood loss exceeds 1,500 ml. Prophylaxis should be stopped within 24 hours.
items.note: The question tests standard antibiotic prophylaxis protocols as detailed in the reference notes.

items.q: To improve the sensitivity of synovial fluid cultures when investigating a suspected chronic periprosthetic joint infection, for how long should antibiotics be discontinued before performing the joint aspiration?
items.e: To avoid false-negative results, antibiotics should be stopped for at least 2 weeks before performing a joint aspiration for culture.
items.note: The 2-week antibiotic holiday is a standard diagnostic requirement mentioned in the reference notes.

items.q: A 72-year-old patient undergoes revision total hip arthroplasty for aseptic loosening. Intraoperatively, the surgeon notes significant wear on the non-articulating 'back-side' of the polyethylene liner where it was in contact with the metal acetabular shell. According to the McKellop classification, this represents which mode of wear?
items.e: Mode 4 wear occurs when two non-intended surfaces rub together, such as the back-side of a liner against the shell, or the femoral neck against the cup rim. Mode 1 is intended bearing wear; Mode 2 is primary surface against a non-intended secondary surface; Mode 3 is third-body wear.
items.note: The question accurately tests the McKellop classification of wear modes as described in standard orthopaedic literature and the provided notes.

items.q: In the biological cascade of particle-induced osteolysis, which size range of polyethylene wear particles is considered the most bioactive in triggering macrophage-mediated bone resorption?
items.e: Polyethylene particles between 0.1 and 1.0 microns are the most bioactive; they are phagocytosed by macrophages, which then release pro-inflammatory cytokines like TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6, eventually upregulating RANKL to activate osteoclasts.
items.note: This is a classic exam fact regarding the pathophysiology of osteolysis.

items.q: During the manufacturing of highly cross-linked polyethylene (HXLPE), the polymer is often heated above its melting point (remelted) after irradiation. What is the primary clinical disadvantage of this remelting process compared to annealing?
o: It leaves significant residual free radicals
It increases the risk of in-vivo oxidation
It reduces the fatigue strength and fracture toughness
It increases the adhesive wear rate
items.e: Remelting (heating above 135-137°C) eliminates free radicals, thereby preventing oxidation, but it reduces the crystallinity of the polyethylene, which leads to lower fatigue strength and fracture toughness. Annealing (heating below the melting point) preserves strength but may leave residual free radicals.
items.note: The trade-off between remelting and annealing is a high-yield topic in biomaterials for orthopaedic exams.

items.q: A 52-year-old active man with a ceramic-on-ceramic total hip arthroplasty presents with sudden onset of hip pain and a 'grinding' sensation. Radiographs confirm a fractured ceramic femoral head. What is the most appropriate management regarding the bearing surfaces during revision?
o: Revision to a cobalt-chromium head on a polyethylene liner
Revision to a new ceramic head with a titanium sleeve and a full synovectomy
Revision to a stainless steel head and a new ceramic liner
Revision to a large-diameter metal-on-metal bearing
items.e: When a ceramic head fractures, microscopic ceramic shards are embedded in the tissues. A metal head should never be used as it will suffer catastrophic third-body wear from these particles. The recommended treatment is a full synovectomy and revision to a ceramic head, typically using a titanium sleeve to protect the head from a potentially damaged trunnion.
items.note: The management of ceramic fracture is a critical clinical scenario with a specific 'never-do' (using a metal head).

items.q: A patient with a metal-on-metal hip resurfacing is being monitored. Which blood metal ion level is generally used by regulatory bodies like the MHRA/FDA as the threshold of concern, necessitating closer clinical and imaging surveillance?
items.e: The threshold for concern for cobalt or chromium ions in blood is 7 µg/L (7 ppb). Levels above this indicate increased wear or edge-loading and warrant closer monitoring with clinical exams and MARS MRI to look for adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR).
items.note: This threshold is a standard guideline-based fact.

items.q: A patient with a well-fixed cobalt-chromium head on a highly cross-linked polyethylene liner presents with a painful cystic mass around the hip. Blood tests show a cobalt level of 12 ppb and a chromium level of 2 ppb. What is the most likely cause of these findings?
o: Adhesive wear of the polyethylene liner
Mechanically assisted crevice corrosion at the trunnion
Type I hypersensitivity to the metal shell
items.e: When cobalt levels are significantly higher than chromium levels (Co:Cr ratio > 3-5) in a metal-on-polyethylene hip, it suggests taper corrosion (trunnionosis) rather than bearing wear. Chromium often precipitates at the junction, while cobalt is released systemically.
items.note: The differential diagnosis of metal ions in MoP vs MoM bearings is a sophisticated and common exam topic.

items.q: Polyethylene wear in Total Knee Arthroplasty (TKA) differs from Total Hip Arthroplasty (THA). Which mechanism is the dominant cause of polyethylene failure in TKA due to low conformity and high contact stresses?
items.e: TKA wear is dominated by fatigue-related mechanisms like delamination and pitting. This is because the low conformity of TKA designs leads to high contact stresses and subsurface cracking, unlike the predominantly adhesive wear seen in the more conforming THA bearings.
items.note: The distinction between THA and TKA wear mechanisms is fundamental to understanding implant design.

items.q: According to Dumbleton, what is the 'osteolysis threshold' for the linear wear rate of conventional ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene in total hip arthroplasty?
items.e: The osteolysis threshold for conventional polyethylene is approximately 0.1 mm/year of linear wear. When wear rates remain below this level, the volume of particles generated is typically insufficient to trigger the macrophage response required for significant osteolysis.
items.note: The 0.1 mm/year threshold is a classic numerical value in orthopaedic tribology.

items.q:
A 76‑year‑old patient with a chronic massive cuff tear and pseudoparalysis presents for surgical consultation. Which of the following is NOT a typical indication for reverse total shoulder arthroplasty?
A. Cuff tear arthropathy
B. Massive irreparable cuff tear with pseudoparalysis
C. Comminuted proximal humerus fracture in an elderly patient
D. Primary osteoarthritis in a 45‑year‑old active worker with intact cuff
items.e: A young patient with intact cuff and an active lifestyle is best managed with anatomic arthroplasty; reverse arthroplasty is reserved for cuff deficiency or elderly fractures.
items.note: Correct answer is D; all other options are standard indications.

items.q: A 22‑year‑old female footballer lands after a rapid side‑step cut. She immediately feels a ‘pop’ in the knee, moves with a mild swelling and reports a sensation of giving way when she turns. Which anatomic factor contributes most to her higher injury risk compared to males?
o: C a medial tibial plateau tilt
D a longer Q‑angle due to a medial tibial tubercle
items.e: Females have a narrower notch, smaller ACL, higher Q‑angle and increased posterior tibial slope, all of which heighten ACL rupture risk.
items.note: Clinicopathologic consensus

items.q: During a clinical exam the examiner performs the Lachman test with the knee at 20° of flexion. The proximal tibia is displaced anteromedially by 6 mm compared to the contralateral side. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?
o: B The ACL has a mild sprain
D The instability is due to a meniscal tear
items.e: A side‑to‑side displacement >3 mm on the Lachman test at 20–30° flexion is diagnostic of an ACL rupture.
items.note: Hall‑mark diagnostic threshold

items.q: Radiographs of a patient with a suspected ACL tear reveal a small, low‑lying fracture on the lateral aspect of the tibial plateau. This fracture is best described as a
items.e: A Segond fracture is an avulsion of the lateral tibial plateau, pathognomonic for an ACL tear.
items.note: Radiographic classic

items.q: A 28‑year‑old male presents with a locked knee after a sudden twisting injury while playing soccer. Plain radiographs are normal. Which imaging modality best demonstrates the likely cause of the lock?
items.e: An MRI shows the presence of a longitudinal bucket‑handle tear, the most common reason for mechanical locking in younger athletes.
items.note: Mature imaging evidence shows MRI is superior for detecting meniscal bucket‑handle tears.

items.q: During arthroscopy of a medial meniscus tear, the surgeon observes an isolated tear of the posterior root. Which intra‑articular finding on MRI is most characteristic of this injury?
o: Ghost meniscus sign on sagittal view
items.e: Root tears produce significant meniscal extrusion (>3 mm) and loss of the normal hoop‑stress configuration.
items.note: Root tears are uniquely associated with extrusion.

items.q: Which measurement on a true lateral radiograph is most reliable for diagnosing patella alta in a skeletally immature patient?
items.e: The Blackburne–Peel ratio uses the tibial plateau line and is not affected by tibial tubercle position, making it ideal for assessing patella alta.
items.note: Patellar height index choice

items.q: In a CT scan of a patient with recurrent lateral patellar instability, the trochlea shows a crossing sign, a supratrochlear spur, and a double contour. According to Dejour, this corresponds to which type?
items.e: All three deforming features together describe Dejour type D trochlear dysplasia.
items.note: Dejour classification

items.q: A 22‑year‑old rugby player presents after a first‑time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation. Arthroscopic evaluation shows a 28% anteroinferior glenoid rim loss and a Hill–Sachs lesion whose width exceeds the glenoid track. Which surgical procedure is most appropriate?
items.e: The 28 % glenoid bone loss exceeds the critical 20–25 % threshold, and the Hill–Sachs is off‑track; thus a bone block procedure (open Latarjet) is indicated. The open Latarjet restores bone stock and provides a sling effect, reducing recurrence. Options A and B (arthroscopic Bankart ± remplissage) are inadequate for >25 % bone loss, and option D is irrelevant to anterior instability.
items.note: Missing correct answer, correction needed

items.q: A 30‑year‑old swimmer has recurrent anterior instability after a primary arthroscopic Bankart repair. On arthroscopy a minor, medially displaced a lever‑shaped labral tear is noted. The tear is best classified as:
items.e: An anterior labroligamentous periosteal sleeve avulsion (ALPSA) is a medial‑inferior displacement of the labrum with periosteum intact, leading to higher recurrence if not mobilised and repaired.
items.note: Correct answer identified

items.q: A 52-year-old manual worker presents with persistent anterior shoulder pain following an injury. On clinical assessment, which of the following physical examination tests is considered the most sensitive for identifying a tear isolated to the upper portion of the subscapularis tendon?
items.e: The bear-hug test is clinically recognized as the most sensitive examination maneuver for detecting tears isolated to the upper subscapularis tendon. The belly-press and lift-off tests are more specific or evaluate larger/lower subscapularis tears.
items.note: Accurate, factually correct, and well-supported by standard arthroscopy reference texts and provided notes.

items.q: A 48-year-old active laborer presents with a massive, retracted posterosuperior rotator cuff tear with an intact subscapularis, preserved passive range of motion, and no glenohumeral osteoarthritis. Which surgical reconstruction utilizes a thick (6-8 mm) fascia lata autograft or dermal allograft anchored from the superior glenoid to the greater tuberosity to restore superior glenohumeral stability?
items.e: Superior capsular reconstruction (SCR), described by Mihata, uses a thick (6-8 mm) fascia lata autograft or dermal allograft fixed from the superior glenoid to the greater tuberosity. It is indicated in young patients with massive irreparable tears without arthritis and an intact or repairable subscapularis.
items.note: Accurate surgical technique question aligned directly with standard postgraduate reference standards.

items.q: A 38-year-old woman presents to the emergency clinic with severe, acute shoulder pain of sudden onset without prior trauma. Plain radiographs demonstrate an ill-defined, fluffy, cloudy calcific deposit within the supraspinatus tendon. According to the Uhthoff classification of calcific tendinitis, this presentation corresponds to the:
items.e: In Uhthoff's stages of calcific tendinitis, the resorptive phase of the calcific stage is characteristically the most acute and painful clinical phase. Radiographically, the deposit appears cloudy, fluffy, or ill-defined due to vascular proliferation and calcium removal.
items.note: Classic classification question with unambiguous single best answer.

items.q: During diagnostic shoulder arthroscopy, an articular-sided partial-thickness tear of the supraspinatus tendon is identified. Calibrated probe measurement shows the tear depth is 7 mm, involving greater than 50% of the tendon footprint. According to the Ellman classification, this tear is classified as:
items.e: The Ellman classification divides partial rotator cuff tears by location (A: articular, B: bursal, C: interstitial) and depth (Grade 1: <3 mm; Grade 2: 3-6 mm; Grade 3: >6 mm or >50% tendon thickness). An articular-sided tear of 7 mm is therefore Grade A3.
items.note: Strict application of the standard Ellman classification scheme.

items.q: In patients presenting with massive rotator cuff tears disrupting the coronal and transverse force couples, true pseudoparalysis of the shoulder is clinically defined as:
o: Active forward elevation under 90 degrees with full passive range of motion
Complete loss of both active and passive external rotation with the arm at the side
Inability to actively internally rotate past the lumbar spine despite full forward flexion
Active abduction limited to between 60 and 120 degrees with a painful arc
items.e: Pseudoparalysis of the shoulder is defined as active forward elevation of less than 90 degrees in the presence of full passive range of motion, typically occurring when massive tears extend across key force couples.
items.note: Standard, universally accepted clinical definition in shoulder surgery.

items.q: A 50-year-old patient has an irreparable anterosuperior rotator cuff tear involving the entire subscapularis tendon. If a tendon transfer is undertaken, which technique provides the most anatomical line of pull for subscapularis reconstruction?
o: Lower trapezius transfer routed with an Achilles allograft to the lesser tuberosity
Latissimus dorsi transfer routed anterior to the conjoint tendon to the superior facet
Sternal head of pectoralis major passed under the clavicular head and behind the conjoint tendon
Teres major transfer passed superficial to the conjoint tendon into the lesser tuberosity
items.e: For irreparable subscapularis tears, pectoralis major transfer is performed. Passing the sternal head under the clavicular head and behind the conjoint tendon reproduces the anatomical vector of the native subscapularis most accurately.
items.note: High-yield superspeciality surgical technique question with clear defensible answer.

items.q: Following an arthroscopic double-row suture-bridge repair of a large supraspinatus tear, structural re-tear occurs medial to the medial row at the musculotendinous junction. According to Cho's classification of repair failures, this pattern is designated as:
items.e: Cho classifies rotator cuff repair failures into Type 1 (failure directly at the footprint, commonest with single-row repairs) and Type 2 (failure at the musculotendinous junction medial to the medial row, characteristically seen after double-row/suture-bridge repairs).
items.note: Specific, correct superspeciality concept.

items.q: An anteroposterior radiograph of the shoulder is obtained in a 65-year-old patient with long-standing shoulder dysfunction. Which of the following radiographic findings is most strongly suggestive of a massive, often irreparable rotator cuff tear?
o: Critical shoulder angle less than 30 degrees
items.e: An acromiohumeral interval (AHI) under 7 mm indicates a full-thickness rotator cuff tear, while an AHI under 5 mm is strongly suggestive of a massive, highly retracted, and often irreparable rotator cuff tear. A critical shoulder angle >35 degrees (not <30 degrees) is associated with cuff tears.
items.note: Standard radiographic threshold question for entrance exams.

items.q: During a physical examination of a baseball pitcher, the examiner applies a valgus load while moving the elbow from 120° flexion to 70° flexion. Pain is first felt between 70° and 120°. What is this test called?
items.e: B – The O’Driscoll moving valgus stress test is highly sensitive (~100 %) for UCL injury; it is performed by applying valgus stress while rapidly extending from deep flexion.
items.note: Accurate; distractors are close but incorrect.

items.q: A 24‑year‑old sprinter presents with a medial tibial stress fracture (pain along the posteromedial tibial shaft). What is the most appropriate initial management in an athlete who wishes to return to competition quickly?
o: Relative rest and gradual return to training
Open reduction internal fixation with plates
items.e: In low‑risk compression‑side fractures (posteromedial tibia) the standard is relative rest and gradual return to activity; surgery is reserved for failure to heal.
items.note: Low‑risk lesion management

items.q: An amateur triathlete is required to test for doping substances. Which of the following is a banned stimulant that is prohibited for the entire competition period according to WADA?
items.e: Stimulants such as amphetamines are prohibited during competition because they give a performance advantage; caffeine is allowed above 300 mg/day, nicotine/arginine are not banned.
items.note: WADA schedule of banned stimulants

items.q: Which investigation is most sensitive for detecting an early stress fracture that is radiographically occult?
items.e: MRI is the most sensitive and specific modality for early stress fractures, showing bone marrow edema before a visible fracture line.
items.note: Imaging sensitivity

items.q: A newborn born in breech presentation with a flexed, abducted hip and a positive Barlow test. Ultrasound at 2 weeks shows a Graf type IIc hip. What is the optimal next step?
o: Refer for closed reduction under anesthesia
Initiate a rigid hip spica immobilization
items.e: In a Graf IIc hip (alpha 43‑49°, beta < 77°) the head is still reducible; immediate Pavlik harness is the standard management for infants < 6 months.
items.note: Standard algorithm for Graf IIc hips

items.q: A 5‑month‑old infant has a persistent right hip dislocation with a reversed or inverted labrum seen on arthrography (inverted limbus). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Closed reduction with hip spica cast
items.e: An inverted limbus (Graf IV) indicates a dislocated hip that is irreducible by closed means; open reduction with pelvic osteotomy gives the best chance of an anatomic reduction.
items.note: Graf IV hips require open management

items.q: A 5‑year‑old boy presents with a mild limp and refers pain to the knee. Radiographs in AP view show a widened medial joint space and a subchondral crescent suggested by a Caffey sign. Which statement best describes the pathologic process at this stage?
o: The capital femoral epiphysis is undergoing necrosis with interrupted lateral epiphyseal blood flow.
Necrosis is restricted to the metaphysis with an intact epiphysis.
The epiphysis is hyperperfused due to increased vascularity.
The joint space narrowing is due to early osteoarthritis of the hip.
items.e: At age 5 the femoral head depends on lateral epiphyseal vessels; the crescent (subchondral fracture) indicates the initial necrotic phase with reduced blood supply.
items.note: Straightforward application of Waldenström stages.

items.q: In a 6‑year‑old girl with radiographic loss of >50 % of the lateral pillar height (Herring group C) at the start of fragmentation, what is the most likely long‑term outcome?
o: Moderate deformity but acceptable joint congruency
Severe flattening of the head and early osteoarthritis
items.e: Herring C indicates <50 % lateral pillar, predicting poor remodeling and a flattened head (Stulberg V) with early osteoarthritis.
items.note: Established prognostic correlation.

items.q: A 6‑year‑old falls from a low height onto a hard surface. Radiographs show a greenstick fracture of the mid‑shaft tibia with complete displacement of the epiphyseal plate but an intact periosteal hinge. According to the principles of paediatric fracture biology, which factor makes this fracture likely to remodel satisfactorily without surgical intervention?
o: Thick periosteum acting as a hinge
Adequate shaft length for interosseous space
items.e: The intact periosteal hinge permits the bone to act as a clock‑spring, allowing the epiphyseal part to rotate back into place and remodel.
items.note: Factually correct and clear.

items.q: In a 4‑year‑old with short limbs apparent after 2 years of age, there is marked ligamentous laxity, windswept knees and odontoid hypoplasia. Which radiographic finding will help differentiate this condition from achondroplasia?
o: Shortened tubular bones in the metaphysis
Flattened epiphyses of the femoral heads
items.e: Pseudoachondroplasia shows a normal face and skull; achondroplasia typically has frontal bossing and hypoplasia of the midface.
items.note: Consistent with the notes.

items.q: In an adult patient with a traumatic cervical burst fracture of C1 (Jefferson fracture), the Rule of Spence indicates an over‑5‑mm lateral mass overhang on the open‑mouth view. What does this signify?
items.e: An over‑5‑mm overhang suggests TAL rupture, rendering the fracture unstable and usually requiring fixation (C1‑C2 fusion or halo).
items.note: Fact is stated in the reference notes.

items.q: A 24‑year‑old male is brought to the ER after a high‑speed motor vehicle collision. Radiographs show a transverse fracture through the spinous process, lamina and pedicles at T12, with no obvious canal compromise. MRI reveals a tear of the posterior ligamentous complex. The most appropriate initial management is:
o: Posterior short‑segment fixation with pedicle screws at T11 and L1
External thoracolumbar brace with close observation
items.e: The fracture is a ligamentous (B2) Chance injury. Ligamentous injuries need surgical fixation; a short‑segment posterior construct suffices if the fracture is isolated.
items.note: Correct, single‑best answer identified

items.q: Which of the following is the investigation of choice to assess posterior ligamentous complex integrity in a thoracolumbar fracture?
o: Plain radiograph of the thoracolumbar spine
CT scan of the involved levels
X‑ray lateral view of the lumbar spine
items.e: MRI STIR best visualises soft‑tissue oedema and PLC disruption; CT misses ligamentous injury.
items.note: Correct, single‑best answer
