items.q: A 62‑year‑old presents with progressive hand clumsiness and a broad‑based unsteady gait. MRI shows a single level T2 hyperintensity in the cervical cord at C6–C7 with no evidence of myelomalacia. Which severity score would correctly categorize his condition as moderate?
items.e: The modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association score ranges 0–18. A score of 13–14 is considered moderate DCM. Nurick grades are unrelated to the mJOA scoring system.
items.note: Clear single choice with correct criteria from the notes

items.q: A 55‑year‑old male with cervical spondylosis has a Torg–Pavlov ratio of 0.75 on lateral radiograph at C5. What does this figure represent?
o: Disc height over vertebral body width
items.e: The Torg–Pavlov ratio is the ratio of the anteroposterior canal diameter to the vertebral body width; values <0.8 indicate relative stenosis.
items.note: Directly matches the definition in the notes

items.q: During pre‑operative planning for a patient with a continuous segmental OPLL at C4–C6, the ‘K‑line’ is evaluated. Which statement best describes its significance?
o: It predicts the risk of intra‑operative bleeding
It determines if anterior decompression will fail
It measures the facet hypertrophy extent
items.e: A K‑line negative (OPLL crossing the line) suggests posterior decompression alone is unlikely to decompress the cord; an anterior approach or fusion is indicated.
items.note: Matches guideline recommendation cited in the notes

items.q: A 45‑year‑old woman presents with a 4‑month history of low back pain that worsens on standing and improves when she sits or bends forward. MRI shows an AP canal diameter of 8 mm and a disc bulge at L4‑L5. What is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism causing her neurogenic claudication?
o: Compression of obturator nerve by an anterior disc protrusion
Hypertrophied facet joints and ligamentum flavum with disc bulge narrowing the central canal
Epidural lipomatosis compressing the cauda equina
items.e: The classic mechanism in lumbar spinal stenosis is a combination of disc bulge, facet hypertrophy and ligamentum flavum thickening that narrows the central canal. This explains the improvement on forward flexion.
items.note: All facts match Campbell’s and the notes.

items.q: A 38‑year‑old man has a right‐sided L4‑L5 herniated nucleus pulposus that is paracentral. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
items.e: A paracentral L4‑L5 herniation compresses the traversing L5 root, not the exiting L4 root.
items.note: Supported by the anatomical table in the notes.

items.q: A 12‑year‑old girl with a 28° right thoracic curve (Risser 1) and menarche occurring 6 months later presents for the first time. Which treatment is the most appropriate initial step?
items.e: With a curve <45° and ongoing growth (Risser 1), bracing is the standard initial treatment; short‑term nighttime braces are for isolated lumbar curves—not the right thoracic curve described here.
items.note: Consistent with SRS guidelines; single correct answer

items.q: A 12‑year‑old boy with sudden onset back pain and a butterfly‑shaped kyphosis at the thoracolumbar junction is found to have isolated facet joint separation on dynamic radiographs. According to Rajasekaran’s ‘spine at risk’ criteria, this sign:
o: Is associated with late‑onset paraplegia only
items.e: Facet separation is one of the spine‑at‑risk signs; when present, it signals a risk of progressive kyphosis and often mandates surgical intervention.
items.note: Clear correct answer; rest are wrong.

items.q: A 58‑year‑old man with known metastatic renal cell carcinoma presents with sudden onset thoracic back pain and worsening right-sided upper‑extremity weakness. MRI shows a posterolateral mass destroying the T6 pedicle with no disc involvement and an epidural compressive component (Bilsky grade 1c). Which sequence is most appropriate to confirm the tumour’s hypervascular nature before any intervention?
items.e: Hypervascular tumours such as renal cell carcinoma and thyroid metastases are best visualised on contrast‑enhanced CT, which also guides pre‑operative embolisation.
items.note: Correct sequencing check

items.q: A 70‑year‑old female with breast cancer presents with acute paraparesis. Whole‑spine MRI reveals compression of the cord at L2–L3 by a lytic vertebral body lesion. Her Tokuhashi score is 10. What is the recommended management strategy?
o: SBRT to the affected levels with a 3‑mm safety margin
Posterior instrumentation plus 3‑mm separation surgery then SBRT
Definitive surgery (posterior instrumentation and tumour excision)
items.e: A Tokuhashi score of 10 (~6–12 months survival) and radiosensitive breast cancer favour separation surgery plus SBRT; definitive en‑bloc excision is usually avoided in metastatic disease.
items.note: Appropriate guideline‑based treatment check

items.q: A 58‑year‑old male with chronic low back pain reports a forward stooping posture and sharp pain after standing for 30 minutes. Standing radiographs show an SVA of 6 cm, PT of 24°, LL of 28°, and PI of 58°. Which of the following is the most likely anatomical culprit for his pain?
items.e: With a PI of 58° the patient needs about 58° ± 10° of Lordosis, but the lumbar lordosis is only 28°. The PI‑LL mismatch (> 30°) forces the pelvis to retrovert (PT 24°) to keep the C‑7 plumb line over the pelvis, leading to pain.
items.note: All facts match the notes and the answer is the only defensible choice.

items.q: A patient with a high pelvic incidence (PI = 70°) undergoes lumbar fusion to L5‑S1. Postoperatively the surgeon notes that the patient’s LL is now 40°. Which statement best explains the risk of future sagittal imbalance?
o: High PI predicts a need for ≥ 70° LL, so the fusion may be under‑lordosed.
There is no risk because LL automatically adapts to the new disc height.
A low PI requires more lumbar lordosis, so the patient is now over‑lordosed.
Posterior column shortening will increase PT, correcting the mismatch.
items.e: A PI of 70° means the optimal LL is about 70° ± 10°. With only 40° LL the patient is now severely under‑lordosed, predisposing to sagittal imbalance and compensatory pelvic retroversion.
items.note: The reasoning is consistent with the PI‑LL target in the notes.

items.q: In a patient with a stiff lumbar spine undergoing THA, the acetabular cup is placed at 42° inclination and 20° anteversion. The surgeon decides to use a dual‑mobility cup. What is the primary reason for this choice?
o: To reduce the risk of heterotopic ossification
To minimise the risk of dislocation in the presence of spinopelvic stiffness
items.e: Stiff lumbar spine alters the functional (spinopelvic) orientation, increasing posterior dislocation risk. Dual‑mobility cups provide a larger jump distance and a greater arc of stability, mitigating this risk.
items.note: Correct per Campbell and notes.

items.q: Which acqetal cup position falls into the ‘death zone’ according to the Wasielewski quadrant system?
items.e: The anterosuperior quadrant lies adjacent to the external iliac vessels and is considered a “death zone” for screw placement due to injury risk to the external iliac artery and vein.
items.note: Matches standard anatomical teaching.
